source.title_on_document: When ChatGPT is gone: Creativity reverts and homogeneity persists

supplement.where: Appendix at the end of the PDF, pp. 28-30, referred to on p. 7 ('see appendix for the rest'). The preregistration is at https://osf.io/hea8r (p. 4); it is not described in the paper.
supplement.holds: The remaining panels of Figures 2a and 2b: AUT recognition accuracy for novelty and usefulness (p. 28), and Task 2 public favor and market success (p. 29) and content quality (p. 30), each with P values by day. No SDs or SEs appear anywhere in the document.

paper_design_summary: Sixty-one college students were randomly assigned to use ChatGPT 4.0 (n = 31) or to work alone (n = 30) in a seven-day lab experiment. Each day they did an alternative uses test (AUT) and a product problem-solving task; everyone worked without ChatGPT on Day 1 (baseline) and Day 7, the treatment group had ChatGPT on Days 2 to 6, and a follow-up survey one month later (Day 30) gave one more AUT (a sponge) and no problem-solving task, without ChatGPT. Blind raters scored each AUT idea's novelty and usefulness and each solution's creativity (tested as 'novelty', next to a Task 2 'usefulness' score, in Table 1), content quality, public favor, and market success; flexibility was a count of idea categories; and SBERT cosine similarity, string matching, and UMAP dispersion measured how alike the answers within each group were.

studies.label: Seven-day lab experiment with Day 30 follow-up (AUT and product problem-solving)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Use of ChatGPT 4.0 on the two creative tasks of Days 2 to 6 versus completing the same tasks without ChatGPT
assignment.quote: After consenting to the study, they were randomly assigned to one of two conditions: ChatGPT use (the treatment group, n = 31) and no ChatGPT use (the control group, n = 30).

arms.name: ChatGPT use (treatment; 'GPT' in tables, 'Experimental' in figures, Group E)
arms.description: Given ChatGPT 4.0 to help finish the two creative tasks on Days 2 to 6; no ChatGPT on Day 1, Day 7, and Day 30

arms.name: No ChatGPT use (control; Group C)
arms.description: Completed the same two creative tasks as the treatment group, by themselves, on Days 1 to 7, and one AUT (sponge) without ChatGPT in the Day 30 follow-up survey

participants.exclusions: None reported. The 61 students enrolled and randomly allocated (p. 3) are the 61 who 'completed the lab experiment' (Section 2.1, p. 4), and the Table 1 note gives N=61 for the whole table, Day 30 rows included. Per-arm counts appear only in the assignment sentence (31 and 30). With no dropouts reported, the same 31 and 30 were analyzed for Days 1 to 7. The paper does not state how many people took the Day 30 follow-up survey, so Day 30 records should not assume 31 and 30.
participants.who: College students with 31 different majors from a university (undergraduates, graduates, and Ph.D. candidates, p. 24); mean age 21.56 (SD 2.62); 36 female
participants.quote: Sixty-one college students (Mage = 21.56 years, SD = 2.62) with 31 different majors from a university completed the lab experiment (per-registered at https://osf.io/hea8r). 36 of them were female.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 12, Table 1 note (N=61); p. 24, Section 4.2

ai_tool.how_used: Treatment participants were provided ChatGPT 4.0 'to help them to finish the creative tasks' on Days 2 to 6 (p. 5). The paper does not describe prompts, instructions, or limits on use.

task.description: Two tasks each day of the seven-day experiment, in counterbalanced order: (1) a low-complexity AUT listing creative uses for an everyday object (e.g., a pen or a brick); (2) a high-complexity problem-solving task proposing new functions or solutions for a company's product (e.g., VR glasses), which is idea generation. The Day 30 follow-up survey gave only an AUT (a sponge), so Task 2 has no Day 30 data (Table 2b; Table 3 '/'). The paper gives the number of tasks inconsistently: 16 (p. 3), 14 (p. 4), and 8 AUT plus 7 product tasks (p. 24).
task.duration: AUT: at most 3 minutes; Task 2: no time limit. Seven consecutive days ('without intervals') plus a follow-up survey one month later (Day 30).

outcomes.name: AUT (Task 1) novelty, Days 2 to 6 (ChatGPT available to the treatment group)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two raters, blind to purpose and condition and following the consensual assessment technique, rated each extracted AUT idea for novelty ('the originality of the idea'); a participant's novelty is the sum of the idea scores, so it also rises with the number of ideas (ICCs >= .90). The AUT raters' background is not stated. Groups compared by t-tests run with the R packages broom and dplyr, one test per day (Welch or Student not stated).

contrasts.reported: Table 2a novelty, Control vs GPT: Day 2 30.77 vs 41.55; Day 3 28.37 vs 40.58; Day 4 17.17 vs 35.32; Day 5 18.17 vs 41.44; Day 6 14.80 vs 39.84. Table 1 (Estimate = Control minus GPT, Statistic, P Value): Day 2 -10.78, -2.21, 0.031 (*); Day 3 -12.21, -2.60, 0.012 (*); Day 4 -18.16, -3.51, 0.001 (**); Day 5 -23.27, -4.34, 0.000 (***); Day 6 -25.04, -4.84, 0.000 (***). Figure 2a P: 0.031, 0.012, 0.0012, 1e-04, 2.4e-05. Baseline Day 1 (no AI in either arm): 7.50 vs 8.78; -1.28, -0.90, 0.373 (ns). No SDs or per-day ns printed; Figure 2a bars carry error bars that the paper does not define.
contrasts.locator: p. 8, Table 2a; p. 11, Table 1; p. 9, Figure 2a

outcomes.name: Task 2 (problem-solving) novelty rating ('Creativity' in Table 2b), Days 2 to 6 (ChatGPT available to the treatment group)
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Two raters 'who had rich work experiences on new project development', blind to purpose and condition, rated each solution (ICCs >= .90); the scale is not stated. The paper's labels conflict. Section 2.3 lists rating (1) as 'creativity (i.e., the novel and useful level of idea)' and Table 2b heads the column 'Creativity', but Table 1 and Figure 2b test the same score as 'novelty' (the Table 1 estimates equal the Table 2b differences, e.g., Day 2 2.83 - 3.82 = -0.99, and the Figure 2b 'Novelty' bars follow the Table 2b means), next to a separate Task 2 'usefulness' score. Coded novelty, following the labels of the analysis, on the reading that rating (1) was scored as novelty and usefulness, as in the AUT. S1-O5, S1-O10, and S1-O13 follow the same reading. The text does not settle it (open question), so the primary with_ai record for this paper should not rest on this label.

outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Reported as Task 2 'usefulness' in Table 1 and Figure 2b. outcomes.name: Semantic similarity (SBERT) of AUT answers within each group, Days 2 to 6 (ChatGPT available to the treatment group)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: Cosine similarity of SBERT sentence embeddings for two answers at a time, averaged within each group and day (MC, ME); higher similarity means less diversity, so direction is coded on diversity (sign reversed). Robustness variants on the same answers: string-matching 'redundancy' (shared character sequences longer than two characters; Table 3, lexical overlap), and set-level dispersion of the SBERT embeddings after PCA (30 components), UMAP (2 components), and min-max scaling: standard deviation, sum of eigenvalues, and ellipse area per group and day (Table 4a, no tests).

diversity_detail.uncertainty: Not described. The text gives 'ps ≤ .01' for Days 2 to 6 without naming the test or what it treats as independent; the Table 3 note ('Numbers in bold are not significant, while the rests are significant (p ≤ .001)') has no bold cells.

company_involvement.description: Coauthor Jihao Huang is affiliated with Beijing Yuxin Technology Company. The document states no role for the company and has no funding or acknowledgment statement.

eligibility.reason: Individuals were randomly assigned to ChatGPT 4.0 or no ChatGPT on AUT and product problem-solving tasks (p. 4, Section 2.1; Figure 1, p. 5). All 61 enrolled students were randomized (31 ChatGPT, 30 control; pp. 3-4), and the same 61 completed the seven-day experiment and were analyzed (p. 4; Table 1 note 'N=61', p. 12): above 50, but not by much. Outcomes are blind ratings of each AUT idea and each solution, a count of idea categories, and SBERT similarity of the answers (pp. 6, 13-16). The paper does not state how many took the Day 30 follow-up, which affects only the Day 30 records. The document screened is the 2024 preprint of the 2026 journal article that c012 names. The search record describes the same seven-day experiment in the journal version, which has not been checked.

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT on Days 2 to 6, the treatment group scored higher on AUT novelty (Day 6: 39.84 vs 14.80; t = -4.84, P 0.000; Table 2a p. 8, Table 1 p. 11) and on the expert rating of solution novelty ('Creativity' in Table 2b), but not on Day 7 without ChatGPT (AUT novelty 17.60 vs 13.02, P 0.053; solution novelty P 0.122; Tables 2a and 2b p. 8, Table 1 pp. 11-12), while its AUT answers stayed more similar at Day 30 (SBERT 0.39 vs 0.33, p ≤ .001; p. 14, Table 3 p. 16).
open_questions: Version: the search record now gives c012 as the journal article Zhou, Liu, Huang & Li (2026), Technology in Society 84, 103087, with this preprint as an earlier version. Its unverified search notes say the journal version reports 3,593 ideas (this preprint: 3302), 427 solutions, and two follow-ups (this preprint: one). The journal version should be obtained and checked before extraction, because its counts and statistics may differ.
Day 30 AUT novelty: Table 1 gives Estimate -3.69, Statistic -2.12, P 0.038 (*), but the Table 2a means are 2.40 vs 2.56 and the text (p. 7) reports no significant difference. Which is correct?

open_items.item: Version: c012 is the 2026 Technology in Society article (Zhou et al., 84, 103087), but the PDF screened is the 2024 arXiv preprint 2401.06816. Unverified search notes give the journal version 3,593 ideas, 427 solutions, and two follow-ups (preprint: 3302 ideas, 427 solutions, one follow-up). The randomization, the 61 people, and the rated outputs belong to the same seven-day experiment, so the journal version matters for the extracted numbers, not for the three criteria.

Day 30 AUT novelty (open question on Day 30 novelty and the unresolved reconciliation difference on S1-O9): Table 1 gives Estimate -3.69, Statistic -2.12, P 0.038, but the Table 2a means are 2.40 vs 2.56 and the text reports no significant difference. The direction treatment_higher is provisional. If the journal version keeps the conflict, the authors or posted data.
Day 30 AUT usefulness: the Table 1 estimate (-6.26) does not equal the Table 2a difference (5.62 vs 5.55).
Day 7 Task 2 usefulness is significant in Table 1 and Figure 2b (P 0.021), but the text says all Day 7 p-values were insignificant.

Task 2 rating (1) is 'creativity' in Section 2.3 and Table 2b but 'novelty' in Table 1 and Figure 2b. The final form codes it novelty. The answer decides whether a Task 2 outcome becomes the primary with_ai record. Criterion 3 holds either way.
How Task 2 'usefulness' was rated: it appears in Table 1 and Figure 2b but not among the four ratings of Section 2.3 or in Table 2b. If the journal version does not say, the authors.
The notes under Tables 2a, 2b, and 3 call every unbolded number significant at p ≤ .001, which Table 1 and the text contradict. The form takes tests from Table 1 and the text, not from these notes.
Figure 2a Day 1 novelty bars (about 15 and 17) do not match the Table 2a Day 1 means (7.50 and 8.78). Day 1 is a pre-treatment baseline kept only as context.

Text values on pp. 14-15 differ from Table 3: Day 1 string matching is given as the SBERT values (0.36 vs 0.35; Table 3: 3.44 vs 3.51), and the text's SBERT and string-matching ranges do not match Table 3. The form records Table 3.

Which pairs of answers enter SBERT similarity and string matching, and which test, on what units, gave 'ps ≤ .01' and 'p ≤ .001'. A diversity standard error needs it (codebook sections 10 and 11). If the journal version does not say, the authors or posted data.

Figures 2a and 2b have error bars the paper does not define, and participant-level arm SDs or SEs of the creativity scores are not printed (pp. 8-12 and 28-30). Tables 4a and 4b print SDs only for the projected semantic embeddings (pp. 16-17). Participant-level arm SDs of the creativity scores are the preferred standardizer (codebook section 9).
How many people took the Day 30 follow-up survey, by arm. Criterion 2 rests on the 61 analyzed for Days 1 to 7, so this count matters only for the Day 30 records.
The preregistration (osf.io/hea8r) is not described in the paper, and no primary outcome is named. The OSF page would settle it.
Task 2 dispersion (Table 4b) and Day 7 AUT dispersion (Table 4a) contradict the claim on p. 17 of less dispersion with ChatGPT. The form codes direction from the tables.
The number of tasks differs across the paper: 16 (p. 3), 14 (p. 4), and 8 AUT plus 7 product tasks (p. 24). No coded outcome depends on it.
